quiz.q: Why did historical friction arise between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles in the Indian constitutional framework?
options: Fundamental Rights reflect individualist liberal philosophy, whereas Directive Principles are inspired by egalitarian socialist goals.
Fundamental Rights were designed to be temporary, while Directive Principles were created as permanent constitutional objectives.
Fundamental Rights lack judicial enforcement mechanisms, while Directive Principles can be directly enforced through Article 32.
Fundamental Rights apply exclusively to private citizens, whereas Directive Principles impose binding restrictions on state actions.
quiz.why: Fundamental Rights are primarily civil liberties rooted in liberalism, while Directive Principles embody a socialist vision for an egalitarian society. This philosophical difference created natural friction between individual liberty and state welfare policies.

quiz.q: How did the Supreme Court in the Golaknath case (1967) prevent Parliament from abridging Fundamental Rights?
options: It struck down the amending procedure under Article 368 as inherently unconstitutional and void.
It held that constitutional amendments under Article 368 fall within the meaning of 'law' under Article 13(2).
It ruled that Directive Principles automatically override Fundamental Rights during any national socio-economic crisis.
It established that Fundamental Rights can only be amended if approved by a national referendum.
quiz.why: The Supreme Court interpreted the term 'law' in Article 13(2) to include constitutional amendments. Consequently, Parliament was barred from abridging Fundamental Rights even through Article 368 amendments.

quiz.q: What essential distinction did the Supreme Court establish regarding Parliament's constituent power in the Kesavananda Bharati case?
options: Parliament can amend ordinary legislation, but lacks authority to alter any constitutional provision.
Parliament must secure prior judicial clearance before introducing any amendment in either legislative house.
Parliament may alter the basic structure provided two-thirds of state legislatures formally ratify it.
Parliament possesses the constituent power to amend provisions, but cannot rewrite the Constitution's core identity.
quiz.why: The Supreme Court distinguished between amending the Constitution and rewriting it. While Parliament possesses broad amending power under Article 368, it cannot destroy the Constitution's basic structure or core identity.

quiz.q: In the Minerva Mills case (1980), how did the Supreme Court restore balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles?
options: By declaring that Fundamental Rights must permanently supersede all socio-economic goals contained in Part Four.
By making all Directive Principles immediately justiciable and directly enforceable in the Supreme Court.
By striking down provisions that gave blanket precedence to all Directive Principles over Fundamental Rights.
By eliminating judicial review over constitutional amendments that seek to advance an egalitarian society.
quiz.why: The Court struck down the 42nd Amendment's extension of Article 31(c), which had subordinated Fundamental Rights to all Directive Principles. It affirmed that both parts are like two wheels of a chariot and must remain harmonized.
